q: A patient had a drug-eluting stent for an acute coronary syndrome 4 months ago. When should elective (not time-sensitive) non-cardiac surgery ideally take place?
why: 2022 ESC: delay elective surgery 12 months after ACS and 6 months after elective PCI. Time-sensitive surgery needs at least 1 month of DAPT after elective PCI (3 months after PCI for high-risk ACS).

q: A patient on prasugrel needs elective surgery with significant bleeding risk. How long before should prasugrel be stopped?
why: Stop prasugrel 7 days, clopidogrel 5 days and ticagrelor 3–5 days before. Continue aspirin after PCI if bleeding risk allows.

q: A patient on dapagliflozin is listed for an elective laparotomy. What is the advice?
o: Omit on the morning of surgery only
why: SGLT2 inhibitors should stop at least 3 days before intermediate- or high-risk surgery because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis.

q: A 72-year-old with ischaemic heart disease has major abdominal surgery. Which post-operative test detects myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS)?
why: Measure hs-troponin before and at 24 and 48 hours after intermediate- or high-risk surgery in patients aged 65 or over or with cardiovascular disease or risk factors; most MINS is silent.

q: A pacing-dependent patient with a permanent pacemaker needs monopolar diathermy above the umbilicus. What is the safest plan?
o: Reprogramme to an asynchronous (fixed-rate) mode or apply a magnet
Use maximum diathermy power to finish quickly
why: Diathermy interference can inhibit pacing. For a pacing-dependent patient, switch to an asynchronous mode (magnet or reprogramming); prefer bipolar diathermy, with the return plate away from the device.

q: A patient has a pacing ICD. A magnet is placed over the device. What effect will it have?
o: Switches pacing to a fixed rate
why: In an ICD the magnet only suspends the defibrillator function; it does not switch pacing to a fixed rate. Pacing-dependent ICD patients need reprogramming. Apply external pads.

q: In ischaemic heart disease, what determines coronary perfusion pressure to the left ventricle?
why: CPP = aortic diastolic pressure − LVEDP. Defend diastolic pressure first (metaraminol) and avoid raising LVEDP with unnecessary fluid.

q: In severe aortic stenosis, which echo change suggests the left ventricle is starting to fail?
o: Concentric hypertrophy with a thick wall
A dilating ventricle with a thinning wall
why: LVH is compensatory (Laplace’s law: wall tension falls as thickness rises). Dilatation with wall thinning means decompensation. Functional status is the key question in AS.

q: By the 2022 ESC/ERS definition, what mean pulmonary artery pressure at rest defines pulmonary hypertension?
why: Pulmonary hypertension is a mean PAP above 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation; pre-capillary if PVR is above 2 Wood units. (Older definitions used 25 mmHg.)

q: During laparoscopy, a patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension becomes acutely hypotensive with a dilated RV on TOE. Which is the most appropriate management?
o: 100% oxygen, hyperventilation, inhaled nitric oxide, and noradrenaline or vasopressin to keep SVR up
GTN infusion to offload the heart
why: A PH crisis presents with hypotension. Offload the RV (100% O2, correct hypercarbia and acidosis, inhaled NO or iloprost), support it (inotrope, noradrenaline or vasopressin, sinus rhythm), give no more fluid, and consider VA ECMO.
